title: Karo
localName: Karo — kalo, kwon kal, millet bread
author: Kaaka Kyomuhendo
desc: Millet and cassava flour mixed three to one, added gradually to three litres of boiling water per kilo, mingled half an hour until it leaves the stick clean, then settled in a flour-lined basket.
longDesc: Karo — kalo in the west, kwon kal in Acholi — is the mingled millet bread, and it is the hardest thing to make well in Ugandan cooking. The reason the cassava flour is there is technical and worth knowing: millet flour alone is coarse and reacts stiffly to water, so it is difficult to turn into a paste, and cassava improves the texture and workability. The doneness cue is the one every mingled starch shares: it stops sticking to the stirring stick.
ingredients: Millet flour and cassava flour, mixed 3 parts millet to 1 part cassava — or bought pre-mixed
3 litres water per kilo of flour
Hot water, for the second addition
Raw flour, to line the basket
steps: Combine the millet and cassava flour in a 3 to 1 ratio, or buy it pre-mixed.
Boil the water — three litres to a kilo of flour.
Add the flour gradually while stirring continuously. Adding it gradually is what prevents air pockets.
Keep working it until the water has reduced by half.
Add more water at that point — and it must be hot. Cold water at this stage makes the flour stiff.
Keep mixing. It takes about 30 minutes, depending on the amount, and you stop when the mixture no longer sticks to the stirring stick.
Transfer it to a basket lined with raw flour.
Shake the basket to let it settle into shape.
Cover it and rest 10 to 15 minutes before serving.
chefTips: No longer sticking to the stick. That is the cue, and it is the same one that governs every mingled starch from posho to atapa.
Three litres of water to a kilo of flour. That is the only published ratio for karo and it is the number to start from.
Cassava flour is not a cheapening of the millet. Millet alone is coarse and stiff in water and hard to bring to a paste — the cassava is what makes it workable.
Add the flour gradually. Dumped in, it traps air pockets that you cannot work out afterwards.
Hot water for the second addition, never cold. Cold water at that point sets the flour stiff and the batch is finished.
Thirty minutes of real mingling. This is physical work and it is why karo is a dish people are proud of making.
Line the basket with raw flour before the dough goes in, or it sticks and you lose the shape.

The source gives the millet-to-cassava ratio two incompatible ways — three to one in its method, and one to three through one to five in its discussion. Three to one is used here and the conflict is stated rather than resolved. Test it before you commit.
In an Ankole family there is a special basket, the endiiro, used by the head of the family, and separate baskets for everyone else.
commonMistakes: Adding the flour all at once.
Adding cold water at the halfway point.
Stopping before it leaves the stick clean.
Putting it into an unlined basket.
sources: Adapted from the Ankole chapter of the Wikibooks project 'Mujje Tulye from Uganda' — one of only two chapters in that book to carry quantities. The three litres of water to a kilo of flour, the 3 to 1 millet-to-cassava mix, the gradual addition to prevent air pockets, the reduce-by-half then add-more-water step with its explicit warning against cold water, the roughly 30 minutes of mixing, the no-longer-adheres-to-the-utensil doneness cue, the flour-lined basket, the shaking to settle and the 10-to-15-minute covered rest are all from that chapter.

Its technical explanation is reproduced closely: millet flour alone is coarse and difficult to turn into a paste due to its stiff reaction to water, and cassava flour improves texture and workability.
That chapter states the millet-to-cassava ratio two incompatible ways — 'three to one' in the method and '1:3 to 1:5' in the discussion. Both are reported; neither is resolved.

It also records that karo is well known among the agrarian peoples of western Uganda including the Bakiga, Banyankole, Batooro and Banyoro, that traditions suggest it originated in northern Uganda before spreading south, that it is served with eshabwe and leafy greens at child-naming and marriage ceremonies, and that in an Ankole family a special basket called the endiiro is used by the head of the household.
Amuna Foods has no written kwon kal recipe — only a TikTok video — so the flour ratio, water quantity and turning technique are not available in text from that source. That gap is real.
storage: Best fresh. It firms considerably as it cools.
reheating: Steam briefly, or eat it cold as many people do.
healthBenefits: Finger millet is exceptionally high in calcium for a grain, plus iron and methionine.
Cassava flour is naturally gluten-free and adds resistant starch.
No fat at all — flour and water only.
Very filling and slow to release its energy.
culturalNote: Karo is ceremonial food as much as a staple: it is what eshabwe is served over at weddings and child-namings, and receiving a pet name in Tooro requires a function where millet and firinda are served for it to count. The separate baskets by seniority in an Ankole household are a detail worth keeping — food and status are not separable here.
